lead: The normal distribution is the symmetric bell curve that appears when many small independent errors add together. It is fixed by two numbers: the mean μ sets the centre, and the standard deviation σ sets the spread. Because so many measurements behave this way, the normal model is used for exam marks, measurement errors, manufacturing sizes and noise. Every question is answered by converting to the standard normal Z and reading one table. Some syllabi call it the Gaussian distribution.
prereq: You need Unit 2 on continuous random variables, expectation and variance, a standard normal table, and Chapter 3.1 for the binomial approximation.

sections.h3: The bell curve and its pdf

blocks.text: A continuous random variable X is normal with mean μ and standard deviation σ, written X ~ N(μ, σ²), when its probability density is the curve below. The symbol σ is always positive; σ² is the variance. The constants π and e are the usual mathematical constants. The density is positive for every real x and its total area is 1.

blocks.where: f(x) is the density at x; μ is the mean; σ is the standard deviation; σ² is the variance; π ≈ 3.1416 and e ≈ 2.7183.

blocks.text: The curve is symmetric about μ: f(μ−a)=f(μ+a) for every a. So the mean, median and mode all equal μ. The standard deviation σ decides the width. About 68.27% of the area lies within μ±σ, about 95.45% within μ±2σ, and about 99.73% within μ±3σ. This is the 68–95–99.7 rule.

With marks X ~ N(60, 8²), about 68% of students score between 52 and 68, about 95% between 44 and 76, and almost all between 36 and 84. The figure shows this curve; its peak is at 60 and its height falls as we move away.

sections.h3: Standard normal Z and table use

blocks.text: Subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation: Z=(X−μ)/σ. Then Z ~ N(0,1), the standard normal. The table gives Φ(z)=P(Z≤z), the area to the left of z. For negative z use Φ(−z)=1−Φ(z).

blocks.where: a and b are the interval limits; μ is the mean; σ is the standard deviation; Φ is the standard normal cumulative probability.

items: Sketch the curve and mark the limits a and b.
Convert both limits to z-scores using z=(x−μ)/σ.
Read Φ at each z-score from the standard normal table.
Subtract the smaller area from the larger area for an interval.

blocks.text: For an inverse problem, the area is given and x is unknown. Find the z with that left-tail area from the table, then undo the standardisation: x=μ+σz. For example, the z with left area 0.90 is about 1.28, so the 90th percentile of N(60,8²) is 60+8×1.28=70.2 marks. Area between two values always uses the difference of two Φ values.

If X₁,...,Xₙ are independent normal, and a₁,...,aₙ are constants, then Y=ΣaᵢXᵢ is normal with mean Σaᵢμᵢ and variance Σaᵢ²σᵢ². For two independent normals, X₁−X₂ has mean μ₁−μ₂ and variance σ₁²+σ₂²; variances add even when we subtract.
Y = Σ aᵢXᵢ,  E(Y) = Σ aᵢμᵢ,  Var(Y) = Σ aᵢ²σᵢ²
blocks.where: Xᵢ are independent normal variables with means μᵢ and variances σᵢ²; aᵢ are fixed constants; Y is also normal.

blocks.text: When X ~ Bin(n,p) and both np and n(1−p) are at least about 5, X is approximately normal with μ=np and σ²=np(1−p). Because X is discrete, use a continuity correction: replace k by k+0.5 for P(X≤k), and k−0.5 for P(X≥k). For P(a≤X≤b) use limits a−0.5 and b+0.5.

The approximation fails when p is near 0 or 1 or n is small; then use the binomial distribution exactly. For rare events use the Poisson model. This approximation is behind many large-sample tests in Unit 6. The bivariate normal is a joint distribution; see Unit 4. For positive skewed data, see the log-normal distribution.

figure.caption: The curve peaks at 60 marks; about 68% of the area lies between 52 and 68.

spec.aria: Bell curve for marks with mean 60 and standard deviation 8, centred at 60.

examples.question: Exam marks X are normal with mean μ=60 and standard deviation σ=8. Find P(50 < X < 70).
steps: The limits are a=50 and b=70. Standardise: z₁=(50−60)/8=−10/8=−1.25 and z₂=(70−60)/8=10/8=1.25.
By symmetry Φ(−1.25)=1−Φ(1.25), so the probability is 2Φ(1.25)−1.
From the standard normal table, Φ(1.25)=0.89435.
examples.answer: P(50<X<70) ≈ 0.7887, so about 78.87% of students score between 50 and 70 marks.
examples.check:
from math import erf, sqrt
mu = 60.0
sigma = 8.0
a = 50.0
b = 70.0
z1 = (a - mu) / sigma
z2 = (b - mu) / sigma
Phi = lambda z: 0.5 * (1.0 + erf(z / sqrt(2.0)))
p = Phi(z2) - Phi(z1)
print(z1)
print(z2)
print(round(Phi(z2), 5))
print(round(p, 4))

traps: Putting σ² in the denominator of the pdf instead of σ: the normal density has σ√(2π) and 2σ².
Forgetting the continuity correction when a binomial count is approximated by a normal curve.
Reading the table as a right-tail area. The standard table gives Φ(z)=P(Z≤z), the left-tail area.
Adding standard deviations for a sum or difference of independent normals. Variances add, so X₁−X₂ has variance σ₁²+σ₂², not (σ₁−σ₂)².
Using the normal approximation when np or n(1−p) is too small; then the binomial shape is skewed and the approximation is poor.

quiz.q: Write the probability density function of N(μ, σ²) and name its two parameters.
quiz.a: f(x)=1/(σ√(2π))·exp(−(x−μ)²/(2σ²)). The parameters are the mean μ and the standard deviation σ, with variance σ².

quiz.q: Why are the mean, median and mode of a normal distribution all equal?
quiz.a: The density is symmetric about μ. The balance point is μ, so the mean is μ. The middle area is split equally at μ, so the median is μ. The highest point is at μ, so the mode is μ.

quiz.q: Use the normal approximation with continuity correction for X ~ Bin(100, 0.4) to estimate P(X ≤ 45).
Machine A fills packets with mass N(500, 5²) grams and machine B with mass N(505, 4²) grams, independently. Find the distribution of A−B and P(A>B).
quiz.a: D=A−B is normal with mean 500−505=−5 and variance 5²+4²=41, so standard deviation √41=6.403. P(A>B)=P(D>0)=1−Φ((0+5)/6.403)=1−Φ(0.781)=1−0.7823=0.2177.

quiz.q: Why does a continuity correction improve the normal approximation to a binomial count?
quiz.a: A binomial count takes whole numbers. P(X≤45) includes the whole block at 45. A continuous normal curve needs an interval, so we use the upper edge 45.5. This includes half the block that would otherwise be missed.
About 68% lies between 85 and 115, about 95% between 70 and 130, and about 99.7% between 55 and 145.

beyond: Not for the exam. In finance, the normal model gives Value at Risk when returns are close to normal, and its failure in fat-tailed markets is a standard warning. In engineering, measurement noise is often modelled as Gaussian, which leads to Kalman filters. In machine learning, Gaussian processes use the multivariate normal; see Unit 4. Search next for the quantile function, the Box–Muller transform, and the Jarque–Bera test.
